Dealing with dickovers (permalink)
One of 2026's better tech-related coinages is "dickover," John Gruber's term for

a modal panel, popover, or curtain presented by a website or app, deliberately obscuring its own content to frustrate the user with an unwanted, unnecessary, mandatory interaction; e.g. asking the user to accept “cookies”, subscribe to a newsletter, install the website’s mobile app, agree to terms of service, or anything else that the user couldn’t give two shits about.
https://daringfireball.net/2026/05/what_is_a_dickover

These are bad everywhere, but they are especially terrible in the UK and EU, where websites practice a form of malicious compliance to the GDPR, Europe's landmark privacy law. Under the GDPR, websites are required to secure your affirmative consent to process your data. The obvious way that websites should respond to this is by not collecting your data unless there's a damned good reason for it, but the actual response is to repeatedly shove cookie-consent dialogs in your face before letting you use the site.

These are absolutely unnecessary. Your browser can be configured to transmit a "global privacy control signal" by default that tells websites you don't consent to be spied on while you look at their pages:
https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/global-privacy-control

But many websites punish you by throwing up a "Global Privacy Control detected" dickover that forces you to click through to affirm their confirmation of your confirmation that you don't want to be spied on.

If you don't have the GPC set, websites will demand that you tell them whether you want to be spied on – and they'll do it again, every time you visit them. The website operators falsely claim that they have to do this under the terms of the GDPR (or other laws, like California's CCPA). This is a lie. Every privacy law contains an exception that allows websites to store data about you for a "legitimate interest," and that obviously includes setting a cookie that says, "don't ever spy on this user."

What's a legit interest? Well, I can tell you what it isn't. Facebook claimed that they had to spy on you, even if you opted out by laboriously clicking through one of their dickovers or by transmitting a GPC signal to their servers, because you had also clicked through their terms of service, which say, "Facebook is going to spy on you with every hour that god sends, from asshole to appetite, abandon hope all ye who enter here" (a direct quote). Facebook claims that this is a contract with you, whereby the company has promised to spy on you, and if they stop, they would be violating the contract, which might make you mad, so they are legally required to eavesdrop on every conversation you have and follow you everywhere you go:

https://www.cliffordchance.com/content/dam/cliffordchance/briefings/2023/07/european-court-of-justice-in-facebook-ruling-clarifies-interplay-between-eu-competition-law-and-data-protections-enforcement.pdf

This is bullshit, and the European Court of Justice affirmed it. But despite the fact that surveillance advertising companies are happy to stretch the definition of "legitimate interest" to cover "spying on you because our ToS say we will," these same companies insist that "legitimate purpose" can't possibly include "remembering the fact that you told us not to spy on you the last time you were here," and so every time you click through to one of many popular websites, you get a dickover, and the only way to make it stop is to "consent" to being spied upon.

But it doesn't have to be this way. While the right answer to this kind of rampant lawlessness is stonking fines and even the corporate death penalty for repeat offenders, internet users have a myriad of options available to them for banishing dickovers to the scrapheap of history. These measures aren't difficult to avail yourself of, and using them will make your life infinitely better, so I'm going to tell you about some of them.

Before I start, one note: these measures only work on browsers, not apps. An app is a webpage wrapped in the right kind of IP law to make it a felony to change how it works, which is why companies are infinitely horny to get you to use their apps, not their websites:
https://pluralistic.net/2024/05/07/treacherous-computing/#rewilding-the-internet

What's more, these measures really only work on desktop browsers, because mobile browsers are apps, and are severely limited by law and mobile operating systems, making it hard-to-impossible to customize them so that they'll respect your rights. This is true of all mobile browsers, but it goes triple for iOS (iPhones and iPads):
https://pluralistic.net/2022/12/13/kitbashed/#app-store-tax

Finally, this mostly only works on Firefox, and it works worst on Chrome, Google's monopolistic browser. When it comes to customizing your browsing experience to get rid of annoyances like dickovers and ads, Chrome is hands-down the worst choice, and Google is about to make it much, much worse, forcing a change that will kill the most popular blockers. Stop using Chrome, switch to Firefox:
https://protonprivacy.substack.com/p/google-is-finally-killing-ublock

So, once you're on your actual computer, using Firefox, how can you disenshittify your internet experience? The first thing to familiarize yourself with is Reader Mode, a built-in Firefox feature that switches any webpage to a black type/white background column of text. Just click the little "page view" icon next to the Firefox location bar or use the key combo "ctrl-alt-r."

Some power tips for Reader Mode: Firefox tries to guess whether a given page should have a Reader Mode option based on its layout. This sometimes blocks Reader Mode on pages that badly need it. You can force Firefox to always allow you to try Reader Mode by going to "about:config" in your location bar, then searching for "reader.parse-on-load.force-enabled" and toggling it to "true". If you switch to Reader Mode and the page breaks, you can switch back by hitting ctrl-alt-r again.

Many websites' "soft paywalls" (which allow you to read an article or two before getting a demand to register and/or pay) can be defeated with Reader Mode. Just hit ctrl-alt-r and see if the whole article appears. If it doesn't, try one or both of: a) reloading the page while still in Reader Mode, and/or; b) Clearing cookies for the page (click the shield next to the site's URL in Firefox's location bar, then click "Clear cookies and site data"), and then reload.

That's Reader Mode, and it comes built into Firefox, and can be installed via various extensions on other browsers. Now let's move on to more advanced techniques, starting with "Kill Sticky," a bookmarklet that deletes any "static" elements in a web-page you've loaded (broadly, this is anything that won't change position when you scroll your browser).

Just click the "Kill Sticky" bookmarklet and all the static elements in the current tab go away. This includes things like navigation bars, which are often (but not always) useless annoyances. The original Kill Sticky, created by Alisdair McDiarmid, is 13 years old, and it still works great, but eight years ago, gala8y created a new version that caught some outliers that the original Kill Sticky missed. I've been running gala8y's version for a year now with no problems, and I recommend it as your second line of dickover defense (after Reader Mode):
https://github.com/gala8y/kill-sticky–forked

Kill Sticky is great for getting rid of the dickovers on a website you're not planning to visit more than once. But if you visit a dickover website regularly, you can permanently block its dickovers by using the Adblock Plus (ABP) browser extension:
https://adblockplus.org/

Once you have Adblock Plus installed, you can instruct your browser never to render a given website's dickover. Just load the website, hover your pointer over the dickover, and click your right mouse-button (Mac users need to ctrl-click). This will pop up a Firefox context menu, and at the bottom of that menu is "Block Element…".

Select "Block Element," then move your mouse around the screen. Different regions of the screen will glow pink, showing you which element (part of the page) ABP can access there. Once you've highlighted the dickover, click the "Preview" button on the ABP dialog in the bottom right corner. This will show you how the page looks after you've banished that element.

If it's an element you want to delete forever, click "Create" and ABP will create a new rule for that page that blocks that element. Note that many dickovers consist of several elements, each atop the other, and after you block one element, you might have to repeat the process to delete the element "behind" it, digging your way down to the actual webpage. Each element you block is listed in the top pane of the ABP dialog box. For example, here's Wired.com's UK dickover:
||media.wired.com/photos/6a565246c8e0799a2981818e/1:1/w_*c_limit/WEB_2026-06-21_EA-WIRED-NBNO-FullQual_0011.jpg

If you block an element by accident and want to restore it, just delete its corresponding line in the Block Element dialog. When websites change their layouts and their dickovers come back, just add the new one to the Block Element for that page. No need to delete the old entries.
Finally, if all else fails, there's Remove Paywall, a website that tries several different ways to load a page without its interrupters, nag screens, regwalls and paywalls:
https://www.removepaywall.com/

It's also available as a browser plugin, so you can just right-click on any page and select "Remove Paywall" from the pop-up menu. Remove Paywall often loads a page with all of its dickovers, and you can use all the techniques enumerated above – Reader Mode, Kill Sticky and Block Element – with Remove Paywall versions of pages.

Back in 2024, Ed Zitron tried an experiment: he bought Amazon's bestselling laptop and tried to use it, discovering it to be a horror-show of shovelware, including processor-devouring preinstalled spyware that rendered it all but unusable:
https://www.wheresyoured.at/never-forgive-them/

Zitron's (excellent) point is that technically proficient people have better computers than most users, and these computers are configured in better ways, and as a result, we participate in a fundamentally different internet to the one that normies are forced to use.
It's an excellent observation, and Zitron's point – that these laptops were actively enshittified by hardware makers and OS vendors – is an important one (the essay is called "Never Forgive Them").

But to this point, I would like to add another: we have a duty and obligation to the people we love to show them how to seize the means of computation. The normies in your life need the tips and tricks I lay out in this article more than anyone. Sure, it takes some doing to install Firefox, Kill Sticky, Adblock Plus and Bypass Paywalls; it takes a minute to figure out Reader Mode.

But if you install these tools for the people you love and show them how to use them (or just reconfigure the sites they visit most frequently to block dickovers and other annoyances), you will permanently improve their internet experience, clawing back hours of annoyances every week, while also protecting their privacy.

Anyone who is confused by switching to Firefox is also going to be confused by the deceptive language and practices that go along with dickovers. By leaving your unsophisticated loved ones exposed to dickovers, you're not decreasing the amount of technological confusion they're likely to experience in a day – you're vastly increasing the amount of danger they face as a result of that confusion.

There's never been a better time to disenshittify your cherished normies' computers. The AI companies' illegal monopolization of the memory market has sent the price of new computers, RAM and storage skyrocketing:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BORRBce5TGw

All of us – but especially normies – are having to do more with less. The best way to squeeze extra performance out of any computer (but especially an aged and underpowered computer) is by switching to a free/open operating system like GNU/Linux and replacing your proprietary, resource-gobbling apps with free/open alternatives:
https://www.fosslinux.com/158206/linux-on-older-hardware-revival-guide.htm

Seizing the means of computation isn't theft, it's bargaining. Commercial surveillance companies will tell you that by spying on you, they are simply engaged in a marketplace exchange in which you swap your privacy for access to online services. But they are running a very curious sort of market: it's a "market" where as soon as you stop to browse someone's wares, the stallholder gets to reach into your pocket and clean out your wallet. In "markets," prices are announced and bargained over, not set unilaterally and extracted from anyone unwise enough to cross the threshold.

Adblocking, dickover blocking and other customizations are a way for you to bargain back, to answer the opening bid of "How about you give me all of your data forever and let me do anything I want with it?" with "How about 'nah?'"
https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2019/07/adblocking-how-about-nah

Dickovers are companies' illegal response to privacy laws. Privacy laws are the public response to companies' out-of-control data theft and weaponization. They call us thieves, but they're the ones who embarked upon a generation-long campaign of unrestricted data plunder. What they call "theft" is just self-defense.

A generation ago, publishers and advertisers fell in love with pop-up ads. Early pop-ups were virulent in ways that are hardly imaginable today: visiting a website summoned dozens of pop-ups, some of them employing dirty tricks like spawning as an invisible 1×1 pixel, or running away from your cursor when you tried to close them. They auto-played sound and music. They were Satanic.

We got rid of pop-ups by installing pop-up blockers. Browser vendors (starting with Opera, then Mozilla) blocked pop-ups by default. Soon, pop-ups simply ceased to exist for the majority of internet users, and at that point, the same companies who'd insisted that they would go out of business unless they could fill your screen with pop-ups quietly gave up on them and found another way to advertise.

No one should ever have to look at another dickover. If dickovers become invisible for everyone on the web, there won't be any dickovers. Companies claim they need dickovers to survive. It's bullshit. They want dickovers, but if dickovers cease to be rendered on their target audience's screens, they'll switch to less invasive tactics, just like they've always done.

这些在任何地方都很糟糕，但在英国和欧盟尤为恶劣，那里的网站对欧洲具有里程碑意义的隐私法 GDPR 采取了一种恶意合规的形式。根据 GDPR，网站必须获得您的明确同意才能处理您的数据。网站应对此的明显方式应该是：除非有极其充分的理由，否则不收集您的数据，但实际的反应是在让您使用该网站之前，反复将 cookie 同意对话框推到您面前。
这些绝对是没必要的。您的浏览器可以配置为默认发送“全局隐私控制信号”（global privacy control signal），告诉网站您不同意在浏览其页面时被监视：
https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/global-privacy-control
但许多网站会通过弹出一个“检测到全局隐私控制”的 dickover 来惩罚您，迫使您点击确认他们已确认您不想被监视的确认。
如果您没有设置 GPC，网站会要求您告诉他们是否想被监视——而且每次您访问他们时，他们都会再来一次。网站运营商虚假地声称，根据 GDPR（或其他法律，如加州的 CCPA）的条款，他们必须这样做。这是一个谎言。每项隐私法都包含一个例外情况，允许网站出于“合法利益”存储有关您的数据，这显然包括设置一个写着“永远不要监视该用户”的 cookie。

什么是合法利益？好吧，我可以告诉你什么不是。Facebook 声称他们必须监视您，即使您费力地点击了他们的某个 dickover 来选择退出，或者向他们的服务器发送了 GPC 信号，因为您也点击了他们的服务条款，上面写着：“Facebook 将无时无刻不在监视你，从头到脚，进入此地者放弃一切希望吧”（直接引用）。Facebook 声称这是与您签订的合同，公司据此承诺监视您，如果他们停止监视，就会违反合同，这可能会让您生气，因此他们在法律上有义务窃听您的每一次对话，并跟踪您的每一个足迹：

https://www.cliffordchance.com/content/dam/cliffordchance/briefings/2023/07/european-court-of-justice-in-facebook-ruling-clarifies-interplay-between-eu-competition-law-and-data-protections-enforcement.pdf
这纯属扯淡，欧洲法院也对此予以了确认。然而，尽管监控广告公司很乐意将“合法利益”的定义延伸到“因为我们的服务条款（ToS）写了我们会这么做，所以我们要监视你”，这些公司却坚称“合法目的”绝不能包含“记住你上次在这里告诉我们不要监视你这件事”。因此，每次你点击进入众多热门网站之一时，你都会被恶心到，而让它停止的唯一方法就是“同意”被监视。
但事情并非必须如此。虽然应对这种猖獗的违法行为，正确的做法是处以巨额罚款，甚至对屡教不改者执行企业死刑，但互联网用户也有无数种选择，可以将这种恶心人的体验扫进历史的垃圾堆。这些措施并不难掌握，使用它们会让你的生活无限美好，所以我打算向你介绍其中一些。
在开始之前，有一点需要注意：这些措施仅适用于浏览器，不适用于应用程序。应用程序就是一个网页，只不过被包裹在特定的知识产权法中，使得改变其运作方式成为一项重罪，这就是为什么公司极其渴望让你使用他们的应用程序，而不是他们的网站：
https://pluralistic.net/2024/05/07/treacherous-computing/#rewilding-the-internet
更重要的是，这些措施实际上只适用于桌面浏览器，因为移动端浏览器本身就是应用程序，受到法律和移动操作系统的严重限制，使得自定义它们以尊重你的权利变得困难重重甚至根本不可能。所有移动浏览器都是如此，而在 iOS（iPhone 和 iPad）上更是变本加厉：
https://pluralistic.net/2022/12/13/kitbashed/#app-store-tax
最后，这主要只在 Firefox 上有效，而在 Google 的垄断浏览器 Chrome 上效果最差。在自定义浏览体验以摆脱恶心人的弹窗和广告方面，Chrome 绝对是最糟糕的选择，而且 Google 即将让情况变得极其糟糕，强制推行一项将扼杀最受欢迎的拦截器的改变。停止使用 Chrome，切换到 Firefox：
https://protonprivacy.substack.com/p/google-is-finally-killing-ublock
那么，一旦你坐在真正的电脑前，使用着 Firefox，你该如何净化你的互联网体验呢？你需要熟悉的第一件事是阅读模式（Reader Mode），这是 Firefox 的内置功能，可以将任何网页切换为黑字白底的文本栏。只需点击 Firefox 地址栏旁边的小“页面视图”图标，或使用组合键“ctrl-alt-r”即可。

关于阅读模式的一些高级技巧：Firefox 会尝试根据网页布局来猜测某个页面是否应该提供阅读模式选项。这有时会导致那些急需阅读模式的页面无法使用它。你可以强制 Firefox 始终允许你尝试阅读模式，方法是在地址栏中输入“about:config”，然后搜索“reader.parse-on-load.force-enabled”并将其切换为“true”。如果你切换到阅读模式后页面出现故障，你可以再次按 ctrl-alt-r 切换回去。
许多网站的“软付费墙”（允许你在被要求注册和/或付费前阅读一两篇文章）可以通过阅读模式来破解。只需按下 ctrl-alt-r，看看整篇文章是否会显示。如果没有，尝试以下一种或两种方法：a) 在阅读模式下重新加载页面；b) 清除该页面的 cookies（点击 Firefox 地址栏中网站 URL 旁边的盾牌图标，然后点击“清除 cookies 和站点数据”），然后重新加载。
这就是阅读模式，它内置于 Firefox 中，也可以通过其他浏览器上的各种扩展程序安装。现在让我们继续介绍更高级的技巧，从“Kill Sticky”开始，这是一个书签小程序，可以删除你加载的网页中任何“静态”元素（广义上讲，就是当你滚动浏览器时不会改变位置的任何内容）。

只需点击“Kill Sticky”书签小程序，当前标签页中的所有静态元素就会消失。这包括导航栏之类的东西，它们通常是（但不总是）毫无用处的烦人元素。由 Alisdair McDiarmid 创建的原始 Kill Sticky 已经有 13 年历史了，它仍然运行得很好，但八年前，gala8y 创建了一个新版本，捕获了原始 Kill Sticky 遗漏的一些边缘情况。我已经使用 gala8y 的版本一年了，没有任何问题，我推荐它作为你对抗强制遮挡层的第二道防线（在阅读模式之后）：
https://github.com/gala8y/kill-sticky–forked
Kill Sticky 非常适合用来摆脱你不打算多次访问的网站上的强制遮挡层。但如果你经常访问一个有强制遮挡层的网站，你可以使用 Adblock Plus (ABP) 浏览器扩展来永久屏蔽它的遮挡层：
https://adblockplus.org/
安装 Adblock Plus 后，你可以指示你的浏览器永远不要渲染某个网站的强制遮挡层。只需加载该网站，将指针悬停在遮挡层上，然后单击鼠标右键（Mac 用户需要按住 ctrl 单击）。这将弹出一个 Firefox 上下文菜单，在该菜单的底部是“拦截元素...”（Block Element...）。
选择“拦截元素”，然后在屏幕上移动鼠标。屏幕的不同区域会发出粉红色的光，向你显示 ABP 在那里可以访问哪个元素（页面的一部分）。一旦你高亮显示了该遮挡层，点击右下角 ABP 对话框上的“预览”（Preview）按钮。这将向你展示移除该元素后页面的外观。
如果这是你想永久删除的元素，请点击“创建”（Create），ABP 将为该页面创建一条新规则来拦截该元素。请注意，许多遮挡层由多个元素组成，彼此叠加在一起，在你拦截一个元素后，你可能需要重复此过程来删除它“背后”的元素，一路向下挖掘直到看到实际的网页。你拦截的每个元素都列在 ABP 对话框的顶部窗格中。例如，这是 Wired.com 英国版的强制遮挡层：
||media.wired.com/photos/6a565246c8e0799a2981818e/1:1/w_*c_limit/WEB_2026-06-21_EA-WIRED-NBNO-FullQual_0011.jpg
如果你意外拦截了某个元素并想要恢复它，只需在“拦截元素”对话框中删除其对应的行。当网站更改其布局并且其遮挡层再次出现时，只需将新的遮挡层添加到该页面的“拦截元素”中即可。无需删除旧条目。
最后，如果所有其他方法都失败了，还有 Remove Paywall 这个网站，它会尝试几种不同的方法来加载页面，并去除其中的中断程序、烦人的提示屏幕、注册墙和付费墙：
https://www.removepaywall.com/
它也可以作为浏览器插件使用，因此你只需在任何页面上右键单击，并从弹出菜单中选择“Remove Paywall”即可。Remove Paywall 通常会加载包含所有烦人覆盖层的页面，你可以将上面列举的所有技巧——阅读模式、Kill Sticky 和 Block Element——与 Remove Paywall 版本的页面结合使用。
早在 2024 年，Ed Zitron 做了一个实验：他购买了亚马逊上最畅销的笔记本电脑并尝试使用它，结果发现它是一个充斥着垃圾软件的恐怖秀，包括吞噬处理器性能的预装间谍软件，使其几乎无法使用：
https://www.wheresyoured.at/never-forgive-them/
Zitron 的（精彩）观点是，精通技术的人拥有比大多数用户更好的电脑，而且这些电脑的配置方式也更好，因此，我们参与的是一个与普通用户被迫使用的互联网根本不同的互联网。
这是一个极好的观察，Zitron 的观点——这些笔记本电脑被硬件制造商和操作系统供应商主动搞烂了——非常重要（这篇文章名为《Never Forgive Them》）。
但在这一点上，我想补充另一点：对我们所爱的人，我们有责任和义务向他们展示如何夺取计算工具的控制权。你生活中的普通用户比任何人都更需要我在本文中列出的提示和技巧。当然，安装 Firefox、Kill Sticky、Adblock Plus 和 Bypass Paywalls 需要费些功夫；弄清楚阅读模式也需要花点时间。
但是，如果你为你所爱的人安装这些工具并向他们展示如何使用（或者只是重新配置他们最常访问的网站以阻止烦人的覆盖层和其他干扰），你将永久改善他们的互联网体验，每周夺回数小时被干扰的时间，同时还能保护他们的隐私。
任何对切换到 Firefox 感到困惑的人，也会对伴随烦人覆盖层而来的欺骗性语言和做法感到困惑。让你那些不懂技术的亲人暴露在烦人的覆盖层之下，并没有减少他们一天中可能经历的技术困惑——反而大大增加了他们因这种困惑而面临的危险。
现在是为你珍视的普通用户的电脑去垃圾化的最佳时机。AI 公司对内存市场的非法垄断导致新电脑、RAM 和存储设备的价格飙升：
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BORRBce5TGw
我们所有人——尤其是普通用户——都不得不在资源更少的情况下做更多的事。从任何电脑（尤其是老旧且性能不足的电脑）中挤出额外性能的最佳方法，是切换到像 GNU/Linux 这样的免费/开源操作系统，并用免费/开源的替代品替换掉那些专有的、吞噬资源的应用程序：
https://www.fosslinux.com/158206/linux-on-older-hardware-revival-guide.htm
夺取计算工具的控制权不是盗窃，而是讨价还价。商业监控公司会告诉你，通过监视你，他们只是在参与一场市场交易，你用隐私换取在线服务的访问权。但他们经营的是一种非常奇特的市场：这是一个“市场”，只要你停下来浏览某人的商品，摊主就可以把手伸进你的口袋，掏空你的钱包。在真正的“市场”中，价格是公开宣布并经过讨价还价的，而不是单方面设定并从任何愚蠢到跨过门槛的人身上榨取的。
广告拦截、反“dickover”拦截以及其他自定义设置是你反击谈判的方式，用来回应那句开场白“你把你所有的数据永远交给我，让我随心所欲地处理怎么样？”，你的回答是“‘不’怎么样？”
https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2019/07/adblocking-how-about-nah
“Dickover”是公司对隐私法的非法回应。隐私法是公众对公司失控的数据窃取和武器化的回应。他们称我们为小偷，但他们才是发起了一场长达一代人的无限制数据掠夺运动的人。他们所谓的“盗窃”只是自卫。
一代人以前，出版商和广告商爱上了弹窗广告。早期的弹窗广告的恶劣程度在今天几乎难以想象：访问一个网站会召唤出几十个弹窗，其中一些使用卑劣手段，比如生成一个不可见的1×1像素，或者当你试图关闭它们时逃离你的光标。它们自动播放声音和音乐。它们简直是恶魔。
我们通过安装弹窗拦截器摆脱了弹窗。浏览器供应商（从 Opera 开始，然后是 Mozilla）默认拦截弹窗。很快，对大多数互联网用户来说，弹窗就不复存在了，在那个时候，那些曾坚持认为如果不能在你的屏幕上填满弹窗他们就会破产的公司，悄悄地放弃了弹窗，并找到了另一种做广告的方式。
没有人应该再看到任何“dickover”。如果“dickover”对网络上的每个人来说都变得不可见，就不会再有“dickover”了。公司声称他们需要“dickover”才能生存。这是胡说八道。他们想要“dickover”，但如果“dickover”不再在目标受众的屏幕上呈现，他们就会转向侵入性较小的策略，就像他们一直以来的做法一样。

articles.titleZh: 关于 EMF Camp 2026 的一些快速想法
articles.summary: 作者分享了参加 EMF Camp 2026 的体验，这次他选择纯粹作为游客参加，而不是像过去三届那样进行演讲。没有了设备故障的焦虑、拉拢观众的社交压力和演讲前后的肾上腺素波动，这种纯粹的参与体验让他感到无比轻松和愉悦。
articles.summaryEn: The author shares their experience at EMF Camp 2026, choosing to attend purely as a tourist rather than speaking as in previous years. blocks.text: I've performed a talk at the last three EMFs - so this time I decided to go purely as a tourist. It made things much more relaxing. No waking up from a stress dream that my laptop didn't work. No casually dropping my talk into every conversation to build up an audience. No queueing for the loos five minutes before going on. No adrenaline spikes or come downs.  It was bliss!

After several volunteer shifts over the years, I also decided to be utterly selfish and do none this year. Again, rather nice being on the customer side of the bar without worrying that I'd cocked up someone's order.

Similarly, I had thought about doing an art "thing" or building something for the badge. In the end all I did was ask my friend Skylar to set up a shortcode so people could ring 26262 (BNANA) for an audio surprise.

To be clear - you should absolutely propose a talk, pitch an installation, and volunteer. It's a great way of experiencing the festival and giving back. But I was exhausted after a 6,379 Km Interrail journey and, frankly, wanted a change of pace.

Everyone has a different EMF. I mostly went to talks and looked at cool art. Some people were focussed on playing all the games. Some gorgeous people were just there to strut about in their amazing costumes. A few people delighted in showing off all their cool toys. It really is about seven festivals in one. I'm still bemused by some of the things - I've no idea what a challenge coin is, I'm hazy about how the various puzzles work, I didn't know about the cool musicians until it was too late.
Still, I came away physically exhausted and mentally refreshed - so a success!
What Worked

We took our 
							Walkie Talkies. So much easier to use Push-To-Talk rather than hoping a text was seen. Worked all the way across the field.

I took 
							lots of Thermal Images
							 - and people seemed to like them!

Handed out a million stickers for 
							OpenBenches
							 - and met several people who'd used and enjoyed the site.
I hired an electric van to lug our stuff. It was quick and easy to charge on the way up and back. Much more relaxing to drive than our enormous camper from last time.

What 
							Almost
							 Worked

We got 
							an inflatable tent
							 so we didn't have to faff 
							too
							 much putting it up. In the end we needed a bit of help (thanks Lucy and Parker). The tent was an excellent size. The blackout stuff kept us reasonably cool and there was good airflow. But, fuck me, sleeping on an airbed in a tent in a heatwave just isn't my scene!

Similarly, dragging our stuff from the car park to our village was a slog. 
							Damien from Hacky Racers
							 gave our kit a lift using his Ghost Rider go-kart which saved my aching back.

The queue for the showers was a bit long - our village members sent back regular queue updates. Once I got in, it was pretty decent. Obviously I felt time pressure to clean up quickly, but the water pressure was decent and there was enough space to hang my pants without getting them soaked. Of course, I dropped my t-shirt into a puddle because I'm incompetent!
It was hard to meet everyone I said I'd see there. I kept getting distracted - sorry if we were due to chat!
What Didn't Work
Some of these are no-one's fault, just circumstances. Others are just not the way I'd have done things.

One of the food stalls served the 
							worst
							 veggie burger I've ever had. No sauce, no veg, no condiments or pickles. Just a bun tasting of sadness. Bleh. Rest of the food was decent for a festival.

Given the heat it was unfortunate that the water pressure was so iffy. There was plenty to drink, but it trickled out slowly at times. Other festivals regularly water the paths to prevent so much dust from being kicked up. That might have helped here.

I'm 
							terrible
							 at remembering people's names - especially if I only met them once a few years ago, or they're dressed as a Furry. As much as I love the EMF badge, I wish it were smaller, lighter, and 
							mandatory
							 for people to wear it in a prominent position. Ideally their forehead.
There's a general lack of signage at EMF. The webmap was useful - but a few wayfinding posts would have helped me and others.
It is loud. Some of the music overwhelmed the people who were speaking on stage. I guess it is hard to put soundproofing in a tent 😆

I'm still on the fence about going next time. Not because of anything the organisers did or didn't do. I just can't stand camping in an actual tent. Small camper vans are frustrating to live out of - even for a long weekend. A big mobile home is a pain in the arse to drive. Perhaps I need a glamping yurt? Or someone to chauffeur me in a tour bus?
In short, wandering in the dark and tripping over guy ropes when I'm desperate for a piss isn't the way I like to spend my time!

I'm also conscious that events like these rely on a steady stream of new blood. Having attended three in person and one remotely, I'm aware that I'm taking up space which could go to someone who would have their mind blown by the delightful madness contained in that field.

Previous years have allowed people to get a guaranteed ticket in exchange for one volunteer shift. This year you needed two shifts. I think that's a great way to diversify the festival and stop it just becoming the same faces over-and-over again.

I know that if I don't go I'll suffer from intense FOMO and will vicariously follow all the social media posts. But I don't know if that will outweigh smelling like a rancid turnip and getting stressed that the queue for the loo will be unbearable.
Let's see what the next two years brings, eh?
Photos
Anyway, here are a few of my favourite photos. Click through to see some more on Mastodon.

translations: 过去三届 EMF 我都做了演讲——所以这次我决定纯粹以游客的身份去。这让事情变得轻松多了。不会再因为梦见笔记本电脑坏了而惊醒。不需要在每次聊天时假装不经意地提起我的演讲来拉拢观众。不需要在演讲前五分钟还要排队上厕所。没有肾上腺素的飙升或骤降。这真是太幸福了！
经过这些年几次志愿者轮班后，我也决定彻底自私一回，今年什么志愿工作都不做。同样，站在吧台顾客这一边，不用担心搞砸了别人的订单，感觉相当不错。
同样，我曾考虑过搞个艺术“玩意儿”或者为徽章做点什么。最后我做的只是请我的朋友 Skylar 设置一个短代码，这样人们就可以拨打 26262 (BNANA) 获取一个音频惊喜。
需要说明的是——你绝对应该去提议演讲、推介装置艺术，或者做志愿者。这是体验这个节日并回馈的好方法。但在经历了 6,379 公里的欧洲火车通票旅行后我已经筋疲力尽，坦白说，我想换个节奏。
每个人的 EMF 体验都不同。我主要是去听演讲和看酷炫的艺术品。有些人专注于玩所有的游戏。一些漂亮的人只是穿着他们惊艳的服装在那里招摇过市。少数人乐于炫耀他们所有酷炫的玩具。这真的是七个节日合而为一。我仍然对一些事情感到困惑——我不知道什么是挑战币，对各种谜题的运作方式也一知半解，等我了解到那些酷炫的音乐家时已经太晚了。
尽管如此，我离开时身体疲惫但精神焕发——所以算是成功了！
奏效的
我们带了对讲机。使用按讲功能比指望别人看到短信容易多了。在整个场地上都能用。
我拍了很多热成像照片——人们似乎很喜欢！
发放了一百万张 OpenBenches 的贴纸——还遇到了几个用过并喜欢这个网站的人。
我租了一辆电动面包车来搬运我们的东西。在来回的路上充电既快又方便。比上次我们那辆巨大的露营车开起来要轻松得多。
差点奏效的
我们买了一个充气帐篷，这样我们就不用太费劲去搭它。最后我们还是需要一点帮助（感谢 Lucy 和 Parker）。帐篷的尺寸非常棒。遮光材料让我们保持相当凉爽，而且通风良好。但是，天哪，在热浪中睡在帐篷里的充气床垫上真不是我的菜！
同样，把我们的东西从停车场拖到我们的营地也是件苦差事。Hacky Racers 的 Damien 用他的 Ghost Rider 卡丁车帮我们运了装备，拯救了我酸痛的背。
洗澡的队伍有点长——我们营地的成员不断发回排队的最新情况。一旦进去了，感觉还挺不错的。显然我感到了快速清洗的时间压力，但水压还可以，也有足够的空间挂我的裤子而不被弄湿。当然，我把T恤掉进了水坑里，因为我太笨手笨脚了！
很难见到所有我说过要在那里见面的人。我总是分心——如果我们本来约好要聊聊的话，很抱歉！
没奏效的
其中一些不是任何人的错，只是客观情况。其他的只是不符合我做事的方式。
其中一个食品摊位卖了我吃过的最难吃的素食汉堡。没有酱汁，没有蔬菜，没有调料或腌菜。只有一个充满悲伤味道的面包。呃。音乐节上的其他食物还算不错。
考虑到天气炎热，水压如此不稳定真是不幸。饮料很充足，但有时流得很慢。其他音乐节通常会往路上洒水，以防止扬起太多灰尘。这在这里可能也会有所帮助。
我极不擅长记别人的名字——尤其是如果几年前只见过一次面，或者他们穿着兽人装（Furry）。尽管我很喜欢 EMF 徽章，但我希望它能更小、更轻，并且强制大家戴在显眼的位置。最好是戴在额头上。
EMF 普遍缺乏指示牌。网络地图很有用——但如果有几个指路牌，对我和其他人都会大有帮助。
那里很吵。有些音乐声盖过了在台上讲话的人。我想在帐篷里做隔音很难吧 😆
我还在犹豫下次要不要去。不是因为组织者做了或没做什么。我只是无法忍受在真正的帐篷里露营。住在小型露营车里让人很抓狂——即使只是一个长周末。开着大型房车又是个麻烦事。也许我需要一个豪华露营蒙古包？或者找个人开着大巴接送我？
简而言之，在黑暗中摸索，在憋尿时被帐篷拉绳绊倒，这可不是我喜欢消磨时间的方式！
我也意识到，这样的活动依赖于源源不断的新鲜血液。在亲自参加了三次和远程参加了一次之后，我明白自己正占据着名额，而这些名额本可以留给那些会被那片场地上令人愉悦的疯狂所震撼的人。
往年人们可以通过做一次志愿者轮班来换取一张保底门票。今年则需要两次轮班。我认为这是让音乐节参与者多样化、避免总是看到同一批面孔的好方法。
我知道如果我不去，我会遭受强烈的错失恐惧症（FOMO），并会通过社交媒体上的帖子来间接体验。但我不知道这是否能抵消闻起来像烂萝卜、以及因为上厕所排队难以忍受而带来的压力。
让我们看看未来两年会带来什么，嗯？

blocks.text: Following up on the previous item today, re: content blockers and ad-blocking, I ran into a weird situation a few weeks ago with my column “John Ternus Should Reverse Apple’s Slide Down the Advertising Slippery Slope”. That article contains this sentence, in Markdown:

And -- at this writing, still "coming soon" -- Apple is
launching [ads on Apple Maps][🗺️].

[🗺️]: https://ads.apple.com/maps
The problem is that anyone reading that article in NetNewsWire saw it rendered like this, with the words “ads on Apple Maps”1 omitted:

It looks like I forgot to finish writing that sentence. NetNewsWire simply omits the hyperlinked words. After a few readers reported this, I immediately suspected the problem was the “ads.apple.com” domain. I’ve never linked to that domain before, and many ad blockers just block any domain that starts with a domain prefix like ads.*.

And that’s exactly what the problem is. I had no idea that NetNewsWire filtered any content whatsoever (and I sort of think it shouldn’t), but DF reader Antonio Germano searched through NetNewsWire’s open-source code and found it in the core.css file, line 49:

38  /*Block ads and junk*/
39  
40  iframe[src*="feedads" ],
41  iframe[src*="doubleclick"],
42  iframe[src*="plusone.google"] {
43      display: none !important;
44  }
45  
46  a[href*=".ads."],
47  a[href*="feedads" ],
48  a[href*="doubleclick"],
49  a[href*="//ads."],

The culprit identified, I dutifully pinged my friend Brent Simmons to report the problem. But then I had to decide what to do about it. I have no idea which feed readers are being used to read Daring Fireball’s feeds, but NetNewsWire is surely one of the most popular, and probably the most popular. It’s the feed reader I use personally. I can’t change the contents of NetNewsWire’s core.css file, so I can’t keep NetNewsWire from stripping out words that link to Apple’s ads.apple.com domain. What I could do is not link to ads.apple.com, like, say by changing my link from ads.apple.com/maps to a shorten-and-redirect URL like bit.ly/4wmXFSE that points back to Apple’s original URL.

But I didn’t do that. I don’t like playing whack-a-mole to work around bugs in other software. I have enough trouble fixing my own mistakes. I also don’t like the idea of showing everyone a “Click it and find out where it actually goes” mystery URL from Bitly rather than the direct URL. It’s a general principle thing, and also a much better policy for links that are meant to last for decades.

What I really don’t like about NetNewsWire’s ad-blocking here is that it just omits the linked text. It doesn’t remove the link but leave the words; it removes the words that are hyperlinked to the blocked domain. I’ve run into this with other content blocking extensions. For example, the Banish extension for Safari, which I recommended back in 2022. At some point a year or two ago, Banish started blocking links to Apple’s App Store domain, and it did so by removing the words that link to the App Store. That’s crazy. I linked to the App Store in my own post recommending Banish, which means if you have Banish installed and read that post, you won’t see the headline of the post (nor be able to following the link). I think there are other content blockers that do the same thing with text that links to the App Store.2

So what do I do about that? Do I stop linking to the App Store? That’s dumb. Do I create custom URL redirects for every single link I make to the App Store? That’s work I don’t need or want to do, and adds a layer of abstraction that confuses everyone who isn’t using a content blocker with such a stupid rule. So I just ignore it. But that means an untold number of readers, who are using such content blockers, are just missing words in my articles whenever I link to the App Store. Well, so be it. Ideally, content blockers “just work” — blocking only things you want blocked, never things you don’t want blocked. Nothing is perfect however. What’s pernicious about blockers that remove the actual words that link to certain domains is that that’s not expected behavior. From the reader’s perspective, it really just looks like an editing error on the part of the website, not a content blocker with an overzealous pattern-matching rule.
Ultimately, though, when you install a content blocker extension, you take responsibility for any overzealousness in what they block.

Let me use this opportunity to make a small personal request. The display ads on Daring Fireball are unobtrusive and limited to one per page. They are also entirely private, and always have been. There not only are no cookies or JavaScript that attempt to track you, but the ads themselves are served from the daringfireball.net domain. I turn down advertisers who request to serve images (or “tracking pixels”, which are just invisible images) from their domains. (Such requests are infrequent, thankfully.) I don’t display the ads in between paragraphs mid-article, a common practice that to me is disrespectful both to the writer and reader. In short, I try to keep the ads on Daring Fireball not merely unobjectionable, but something that actually adds to the site. I actually like the ads in certain high-quality print magazines, like The New Yorker. My goal for the ads on DF is for them to be like that.

In short, I hope they’re the sort of ads readers don’t want to block. I’m pleased to say that most of the ad-blocking content blocking extensions I’ve personally tried do not block ads on Daring Fireball by default. In other cases, they do, but it’s easy to adjust the per-domain settings to allow them. In the previous post, I recommended uBlock Origin Lite (free, a bit complex) and Magic Lasso (paid, much simpler). Magic Lasso does not block ads on DF by default. I don’t remember what uBlock Origin does by default, but it’s trivial to change it to allow them.

If you use an ad blocker and it currently blocks the ads on DF, I humbly ask you to consider taking a moment to tweak the settings to permit them. (If you are using a blocker that strips the ads from DF by default, you can do do me an additional favor and shoot me a short email telling me which one. I’m curious.) If you are the developer of an ad blocker, I ask you to consider allowlisting Daring Fireball by default.

If you are a reader and you really do want to block DF’s ads, please, go right ahead. I find that an odd mindset, but it’s your web browser and your call. No hard feelings. (Please further note that I have no JavaScript code that attempts to detect whether you’re blocking DF’s ads in order to nag you.)

I omitted the Markdown creating a link on the words “still ‘coming soon’” for clarity, to emphasize only the problematic link in my original prose. (Also, it’s fun to use emoji as named link definitions, like in this example.) ↩︎︎

I of course reported this to the developer of Banish, twice, but he never responded. I, err, banished Banish from my own devices, and upon finishing this article, I’m going to update my 2022 recommendation of Banish to un-recommend it. ↩︎

translations: 今天接着上一篇关于内容拦截器和广告拦截的话题，几周前我在我的专栏《John Ternus Should Reverse Apple’s Slide Down the Advertising Slippery Slope》中遇到了一个奇怪的情况。那篇文章在 Markdown 中包含这样一句话：

And -- at this writing, still "coming soon" -- Apple is
launching [ads on Apple Maps][🗺️].

[🗺️]: https://ads.apple.com/maps
问题在于，任何在 NetNewsWire 中阅读那篇文章的人看到的渲染效果都是这样的，其中“ads on Apple Maps”1这几个词被省略了：
看起来就像我忘了把那句话写完。NetNewsWire 直接把带超链接的词给省略了。在几位读者反馈了这个问题后，我立刻怀疑问题出在“ads.apple.com”这个域名上。我以前从未链接过这个域名，而许多广告拦截器会直接拦截任何以 ads.* 这类域名前缀开头的域名。
而这正是问题所在。我根本不知道 NetNewsWire 会过滤任何内容（而且我多少觉得它不应该这么做），但 DF 读者 Antonio Germano 搜索了 NetNewsWire 的开源代码，并在 core.css 文件的第 49 行找到了它：

38  /*Block ads and junk*/
39  
40  iframe[src*="feedads" ],
41  iframe[src*="doubleclick"],
42  iframe[src*="plusone.google"] {
43      display: none !important;
44  }
45  
46  a[href*=".ads."],
47  a[href*="feedads" ],
48  a[href*="doubleclick"],
49  a[href*="//ads."],

找到罪魁祸首后，我尽职地联系了我的朋友 Brent Simmons 来报告这个问题。但随后我必须决定该怎么处理。我不知道大家都在用什么阅读器来阅读 Daring Fireball 的订阅源，但 NetNewsWire 肯定是最受欢迎的之一，甚至可能是最最受欢迎的。它也是我个人使用的阅读器。我无法更改 NetNewsWire 的 core.css 文件内容，所以我无法阻止 NetNewsWire 剥离掉链接到 Apple 的 ads.apple.com 域名的文字。我能做的是不直接链接到 ads.apple.com，比如把我的链接从 ads.apple.com/maps 改成一个像 bit.ly/4wmXFSE 这样的短链接重定向 URL，它最终会指向 Apple 的原始 URL。
但我没有这么做。我不喜欢为了绕过其他软件的 bug 而去玩打地鼠的游戏。我自己的错误都修不过来。我也不喜欢向所有人展示一个来自 Bitly 的“点进去看看它到底跳转到哪里”的神秘 URL，而不是直接 URL。这是一个原则性问题，而且对于那些打算保留几十年的链接来说，这也是一个更好的策略。

对于 NetNewsWire 在这里的广告拦截，我真正不喜欢的地方在于它直接省略了链接文本。它不是只移除链接而保留文字，而是把带有指向被拦截域名超链接的文字都移除了。我在其他内容拦截扩展中也遇到过这种情况。例如，我在 2022 年推荐过的 Safari 扩展 Banish。在一两年前的某个时候，Banish 开始拦截指向 Apple App Store 域名的链接，而且它也是通过移除链接到 App Store 的文字来实现的。这太疯狂了。在我推荐 Banish 的那篇博文中，我自己就链接到了 App Store，这意味着如果你安装了 Banish 并阅读那篇文章，你将看不到文章的标题（也无法点击该链接）。我认为还有其他内容拦截器对链接到 App Store 的文字也会做同样的事情。2

那么我该怎么办？停止链接到 App Store 吗？那太蠢了。为我创建的每一个 App Store 链接都设置自定义 URL 重定向吗？那是我不需要也不想做的工作，而且增加了一层抽象，会让每一个没有使用带有这种愚蠢规则的内容拦截器的读者感到困惑。所以我干脆无视它。但这意味着，无数使用此类内容拦截器的读者，在我链接到 App Store 时，会看不到我文章中的某些字词。好吧，随它去吧。理想情况下，内容拦截器应该“正常工作”——只拦截你想拦截的内容，绝不拦截你不想拦截的内容。然而，没有什么是完美的。那些会删除链接到特定域名的实际文字的拦截器，其有害之处在于这并非预期行为。在读者看来，这真的就像是网站的编辑错误，而不是一个模式匹配规则过于激进的内容拦截器。
然而归根结底，当你安装了内容拦截器扩展时，你就得为它们拦截内容的过度激进承担后果。

让我借此机会提出一个小小的个人请求。Daring Fireball 上的展示广告并不显眼，且每页仅限一个。它们也是完全注重隐私的，而且一直以来都是如此。不仅没有任何试图追踪你的 cookies 或 JavaScript，而且广告本身也是从 daringfireball.net 域名提供的。我会拒绝那些要求从他们自己的域名提供图片（或“追踪像素”，即不可见图片）的广告商。（谢天谢地，这种要求并不常见。）我不会在文章中间的段落之间插入广告，这种常见做法在我看来对作者和读者都是一种不尊重。简而言之，我努力让 Daring Fireball 上的广告不仅无可挑剔，而且能真正为网站增色。其实我很喜欢某些高质量纸质杂志上的广告，比如《纽约客》。我对 DF 上广告的目标就是让它们像那样。

简而言之，我希望它们是读者不想拦截的那种广告。我很高兴地说，我亲自试用过的大多数广告拦截内容拦截扩展，默认情况下都不会拦截 Daring Fireball 上的广告。在其他情况下，它们会拦截，但调整特定域名的设置以允许广告显示也很容易。在上一篇文章中，我推荐了 uBlock Origin Lite（免费，稍微复杂）和 Magic Lasso（付费，简单得多）。Magic Lasso 默认不拦截 DF 上的广告。我不记得 uBlock Origin 默认会怎么做，但将其更改为允许显示广告非常简单。
如果你使用了广告拦截器，并且它目前拦截了 DF 上的广告，我恳请你考虑花点时间调整设置以允许它们显示。（如果你使用的拦截器默认会移除 DF 上的广告，你可以帮我一个额外的忙，给我发封简短的电子邮件告诉我那是哪一款。我很好奇。）如果你是广告拦截器的开发者，我请求你考虑将 Daring Fireball 加入默认白名单。
如果你是读者，并且你确实想拦截 DF 上的广告，请尽管拦吧。我觉得这种心态很奇怪，但这是你的网络浏览器，由你做主。我毫无怨言。（请进一步注意，我没有使用任何 JavaScript 代码来试图检测你是否拦截了 DF 上的广告，以便对你进行唠叨。）
为了清晰起见，我省略了为“still ‘coming soon’”这几个词创建链接的 Markdown 代码，只为了强调我原文中那个有问题的链接。（另外，用 emoji 作为命名链接定义也挺有趣的，就像这个例子一样。） ↩︎︎
我当然向 Banish 的开发者反馈了这个问题，而且反馈了两次，但他从未回复。我，呃，把我自己设备上的 Banish 给“放逐”了，等写完这篇文章后，我打算更新我 2022 年对 Banish 的推荐，改为不再推荐它。 ↩︎

articles.title: Excel column numbering
articles.summary: Excel 的列标签并非简单的 26 进制系统，因为它缺少代表 0 的字符。作者在处理客户宽表格时，需要将 Excel 列标签与列号进行转换，从而发现了这一长期被忽视的数学细节。这一发现揭示了 Excel 列名转换背后的实际算法逻辑。
articles.summaryEn: Excel's column labels are not a simple base-26 system because it lacks a character representing zero. While converting between Excel column labels and numbers for a client's wide spreadsheet, the author discovered this overlooked mathematical detail. This reveals the actual algorithmic logic behind Excel column name conversions.
articles.reason: 揭示了日常工具中隐藏的数学陷阱，适合对算法和进制转换感兴趣的开发者阅读。

fullText.siteName: John D. Cook | Applied Mathematics Consulting

blocks.text: I was working with a wide spreadsheet from a client the other day and I had to convert between Excel column labels and column numbers. I had never paid attention to how Excel labels columns and implicitly thought it was base 26 using letters rather than digits. But then I realized that’s not right.

Excel labels columns A through Z, then AA trough AZ, then BA through BZ, etc. If this is base 26, then does A correspond to 0? That could work for A through Z, but then what about AA? Then you’d have to say the first A corresponds to 26 but the second A corresponds to 0.
Does Z correspond to 0? If so then the column numbers would be 1 through 25, followed by 0, then 27. And it would mean that columns ZA through ZZ are the same as A through Z.
In fact nothing in Excel column labeling corresponds to 0. The labels cannot be interpreted as a positional number system.

There’s a name for this kind of number system: bijective base 26. The concept extends generally to bijective base b for any positive integer b. The idea is ancient, but the name was coined recently. It has also been called k-adic numbering. For most of history it didn’t have a name.

The motivation behind the name bijective base b is that there is a bijection (a one-to-one correspondence) between these symbols and positive integers; there’s no possibility of leading zeros that would keep the mapping from being a bijection, unlike say 7 and 07 representing the same number.
Excel limits
Before 2007, an Excel file could have a maximum of 28 = 256 columns, and so the largest column label was IV.
Then in 2007 the column limit was increased to 214 = 16,384 and the largest column label is XFD.
Conversion code
Converting from column labels to integers is easy; going the other way is a little more complicated.
Tests
The following code verifies the assertions above about the maximum number of Excel columns over time.

assert(num_to_label(256) == "IV")
assert(label_to_num("IV") == 256)

assert(num_to_label(2**14) == "XFD")
assert(label_to_num("XFD") == 2**14)

The conversion routines are not limited to actual Excel labels but work for arbitrarily large integers and bijective base 26 representations. For example, the following code shows that the bijective base 26 representation of Avogadro’s number is MUAEKAUDYDXEWOSDD.

avogadro = 602_214_076_000_000_000_000_000
assert(label_to_num(num_to_label(avogadro)) == avogadro)
print(num_to_label(avogadro))

translations: 前几天我在处理客户发来的一个很宽的电子表格，需要在 Excel 列标签和列号之间进行转换。我以前从没注意过 Excel 是怎么给列打标签的，一直以为它是用字母而不是数字的 26 进制。但我后来发现这不对。
Excel 的列标签从 A 到 Z，然后是 AA 到 AZ，接着是 BA 到 BZ，以此类推。如果这是 26 进制，那 A 对应 0 吗？这对 A 到 Z 可能行得通，但 AA 怎么办？那你就得说第一个 A 对应 26，而第二个 A 对应 0。
Z 对应 0 吗？如果是这样，那么列号将是 1 到 25，接着是 0，然后是 27。而且这意味着 ZA 到 ZZ 列与 A 到 Z 列相同。
事实上，Excel 列标签中没有任何东西对应 0。这些标签不能被解释为一种进位制数字系统。
这种数字系统有一个名字：双射 26 进制（bijective base 26）。这个概念一般推广为任意正整数 b 的双射 b 进制。这个想法很古老，但名字是最近才起的。它也被称为 k-adic 编号。在历史的大部分时间里，它都没有名字。
双射 b 进制这个名字背后的动机是，这些符号与正整数之间存在双射（一一对应关系）；不存在前导零导致映射无法成为双射的可能，比如 7 和 07 表示同一个数字的情况。
Excel 的限制
在 2007 年之前，一个 Excel 文件最多可以有 28 = 256 列，因此最大的列标签是 IV。
然后在 2007 年，列限制增加到 214 = 16,384，最大的列标签是 XFD。
转换代码
从列标签转换为整数很容易；反过来则有点复杂。
测试
以下代码验证了上述关于 Excel 列数随时间变化的最大值断言。

assert(num_to_label(256) == "IV")
assert(label_to_num("IV") == 256)

assert(num_to_label(2**14) == "XFD")
assert(label_to_num("XFD") == 2**14)
转换例程不仅限于实际的 Excel 标签，还适用于任意大的整数和双射 26 进制表示。例如，以下代码显示阿伏伽德罗常数的双射 26 进制表示是 MUAEKAUDYDXEWOSDD。

avogadro = 602_214_076_000_000_000_000_000
assert(label_to_num(num_to_label(avogadro)) == avogadro)
print(num_to_label(avogadro))

articles.title: Podcast Notes: Ed Catmull on David Senra
articles.titleZh: 播客笔记：Ed Catmull 接受 David Senra 采访
articles.summary: 皮克斯联合创始人兼前迪士尼动画总裁 Ed Catmull 在 David Senra 播客中分享了他的管理理念。他强调自己的核心工作是“为团队群体建立正确的互动动态”。这篇笔记提炼了采访中的关键观点，并推荐了其著作《创新公司》。
articles.summaryEn: Ed Catmull, co-founder of Pixar and former president of Disney Animation, shared his management philosophy on the David Senra podcast. He emphasized that his core job was to 'get the dynamics right for groups of people.' The notes distill key takeaways from the interview and recommend his book, Creativity, Inc.
articles.reason: 聆听皮克斯创始人分享如何通过优化团队动态来激发创造力的管理智慧。

blocks.text: Ed Catmull, co-founder of Pixar and former president of Disney Animation, was on the David Senra podcast and I quite enjoyed the interview.
(If you like the interview, you should read his book.)
Ed talks about what he considered his job to be: get the dynamics right for groups of people working together.

To do this, he would pull people out of meetings, make groups smaller, make them bigger, just constantly work on fine-tuning getting the right people together at the right time with the right feedback (without ego).
Granted he didn’t always do it, but that was his goal. He says:

This is so important to get [these group dynamics right] because this is what our product is based on: getting this group of people to work well together. So paying attention to the dynamics of the room is the job. They’re the ones making the movies. I’m not making the movie. I’m just trying to get them to work well together.
When Steve Jobs came to Ed and essentially said, “We’re gonna bet everything at Pixar on Toy Story, and the same week that Toy Story is released in theaters we’re gonna IPO.” What did Ed think?
I thought it was crazy [laugh] I’ve learned a lot in this process. He was right.
I love this frank exchange and Ed’s ability to go from “I thought he was crazy” to “I learned”.

In a creative endeavor, where so many earlier iterations suck, how do you gauge whether you should keep going? Because to keep going can make you seem a tad crazy, e.g. “This sucks — let’s keep going!”
So how do you know whether you should keep investing in it? Ed’s answer:

What’s your basis for proceeding? For me, the basis was: what’s the spirit of the team? Because we all know it [sucks] but if they’re all working together — they’re laughing, and [doing things] together — then you say, “Let’s keep going. Let’s keep trying to solve it.”
I love this. He didn’t say, “You open a spreadsheet and do a cost analysis.” He said he looks at the spirit of the people working on it.
It really backs up what he said his job is: find and help groups of people work together. His attitude seems to be: a group of people with the right dynamics can solve anything.
Ed talks about Pixar’s willingness to take on hard problems because they believed a hard problem led to better outcomes (because few others were willing to do the hard work):

A hard problem is more likely to lead to an interesting film. If it’s easy, then it’s more derivative.
You know how to write a script, you know what the three-act structure is, you know all these elements of storytelling, and you put together all the pieces and you got a story. Is it a great story? Is it emotional? Sometimes yes, sometimes no […]
It’s fairly easy to come up with something that is mediocre — and it’s cheaper too.
If you take on hard things then you need to spend more time trying to figure out how to be different in what you’re doing. So if you take on a hard problem and you just keep pushing at it, then the fact that it was hard is what is going to make it different.
Stated again for emphasis: “the fact that it was hard is what is going to make it different”.
And it’s the execution that’s hard, not having the idea:

If you’re going to make a movie about a rat that likes to cook, that is not a slam dunk.
A lot of people want to keep their projects secret, but this is one where you could tell everybody: “We’re going to make a movie about a rat that cooks!”

His point being: nobody can steal that idea and make it good. Execution is everything there. And if you look at it and say, “Well that’s too hard. How could you make a film about a rat that likes to cook?” You’re skirting the hard work, which is exactly what is going to make you different.
Don’t skirt the hard thing. If you do something that’s hard, that’s the differentiation.
Lastly: I love Ed’s perspective on mission statements:
The reason [we never had a mission statement] is because a mission statement is an answer, when typically we should always be asking questions, like “What are we doing?”

His point being: if somebody asks “What are we doing?” and you immediately go back to the mission statement and say, “Oh, well we’re doing this” that’s not good. It’s better to always be questioning. “Are we doing the right thing? Are we going in the right direction?” You should always be wrestling with those questions.

translations: Ed Catmull，Pixar 联合创始人兼 Disney Animation 前总裁，参加了 David Senra 的播客节目，我非常喜欢这期访谈。
（如果你喜欢这期访谈，你应该去读读他的书。）
Ed 谈到了他认为自己的工作是什么：让团队协作的互动状态保持良好。
为此，他会把人从会议中拉出来，缩小团队规模，或者扩大团队规模，不断微调，确保在对的时间让对的人聚在一起，并给予恰当的反馈（不带个人自负）。
诚然，他并不总是能做到，但那是他的目标。他说：
把[团队互动调整好]非常重要，因为这是我们的产品的基础：让这群人很好地协同工作。所以，关注会议室里的互动状态就是我的工作。电影是他们拍的。我不是在拍电影。我只是努力让他们更好地合作。
当 Steve Jobs 找到 Ed 并明确表示：“我们要把 Pixar 的一切都押在《Toy Story》上，并且在《Toy Story》上映的同一周，我们要进行 IPO。” Ed 当时是怎么想的？
我觉得这太疯狂了 [笑]。在这个过程中我学到了很多。他是对的。
我很喜欢这种坦诚的交流，以及 Ed 从“我觉得他疯了”转变为“我学到了”的能力。
在创意工作中，早期的许多迭代都很糟糕，你如何判断是否应该继续下去？因为继续下去可能会让你显得有点疯狂，比如“这太烂了——我们继续吧！”
那么，你怎么知道是否应该继续投入呢？Ed 的回答是：
你继续下去的依据是什么？对我来说，依据是：团队的精神状态如何？因为我们都知道它[很烂]，但如果他们都在协同工作——他们有说有笑，一起[做事]——那么你就会说，“我们继续吧。我们继续尝试解决它。”
我很喜欢这个回答。他没有说，“你打开电子表格做个成本分析。”他说他看重的是参与其中的人的精神状态。
这确实印证了他所说的自己的工作：寻找并帮助团队协同工作。他的态度似乎是：一个互动状态良好的团队可以解决任何问题。
Ed 谈到了 Pixar 愿意挑战难题，因为他们相信难题能带来更好的结果（因为很少有人愿意去做这种艰难的工作）：

难题更有可能成就一部有趣的电影。如果很容易，那它就更具衍生性。
你知道怎么写剧本，你知道三幕剧结构是什么，你知道讲故事的这些所有元素，你把所有碎片拼凑起来，就得到了一个故事。它是一个伟大的故事吗？它有情感吗？有时有，有时没有 […]
弄出平庸的东西相当容易——而且成本也更低。
如果你挑战艰难的事情，那么你需要花更多时间去弄清楚如何让你所做的事情与众不同。所以，如果你接手一个难题并不断推进，那么它之所以困难，正是它将与众不同的原因。
再次强调：“它之所以困难，正是它将与众不同的原因”。
而且困难在于执行，而不是产生想法：

如果你要拍一部关于一只喜欢做饭的老鼠的电影，那并不是稳操胜券的。
很多人想对自己的项目保密，但这个项目你可以告诉所有人：“我们要拍一部关于一只会做饭的老鼠的电影！”
他的观点是：没人能偷走那个创意并把它做好。执行力才是关键所在。如果你看着它说：“嗯，这太难了。怎么能拍一部关于一只喜欢做饭的老鼠的电影呢？”你就是在逃避困难的工作，而这恰恰是让你与众不同的地方。
不要逃避困难的事情。如果你做的事情很难，那就是差异化。
最后：我很喜欢 Ed 对使命宣言的看法：
[我们从未有过使命宣言的]原因在于，使命宣言是一个答案，而通常我们应该始终在提出问题，比如“我们在做什么？”
他的观点是：如果有人问“我们在做什么？”而你立刻搬出使命宣言说：“哦，我们在做这个”，那是不好的。最好始终保持质疑。“我们做的事情对吗？我们的方向正确吗？”你应该始终在这些问题上反复斟酌。

blocks.text: Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure, and industrial technology. This week we look at China’s EV subsidies, the future of aeroderivative gas turbines, a US-Saudi nuclear deal, defective roadway guardrails, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.
The CEO of DR Horton, largest homebuilder in the US, thinks that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act won’t have much impact on housing supply or demand in the short term. [X]

The Financial Times on why socialists should embrace luxury apartments. “Above all, high-end developments unlock long housing chains. As higher-income households move into newly built units, they free up older properties, raising supply and slashing prices for middle- and lower-end housing through a process known as filtering. Numerous international studies underscore this positive ripple effect.” A good sentiment, though stating it to the readers of the Financial Times is probably preaching to the choir. [FT]

Last week we noted that Saronic, which had been slated to be a major tenant for California Forever’s shipbuilding facility, had instead opted to locate their operations in Texas. Someone claimed on Twitter that California was, in fact, never really in consideration, and that overtures to California Forever were entirely to secure better terms in Texas. [X]
The fraction of housing markets in the US where prices are rising vs falling over time, via ResiClub. [X]
US cities which used to have at least 100,000 people but no longer do. [Reddit]
TSMC is accelerating its investment in Arizona fabs due to enormous AI demand. [CNBC] And TSMC plans to raise prices by up to 10% starting in 2027. [Yahoo Finance]

As China’s EV industry gets more mature, China is beginning to roll back subsidies for the sector. “Starting Sept. 1, lithium-ion batteries will be subject to a 2% consumption tax, which will double to 4% a year later, according to a Friday announcement by the Ministry of Finance.” [X]

The National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) requires considering whether a new project will impact the view of some existing historic property. Thus the more land area a project extends over, or the taller it is, the more potential view impacts, and the greater the NHPA review burden. This is bad news for clean energy projects like wind and solar, which have a much “viewprint” than oil and gas projects. “We examined nearly 100 recent energy projects and found a striking discrepancy: compared to fossil energy projects, clean energy and transmission projects have review areas about 10 times larger and are more than 8 times as likely to receive an “adverse effect” finding — triggering additional process, delay, and mitigation obligations.” [IFP]

Tim Latimer, CEO of geothermal startup Fervo Energy, on what the geothermal industry can learn from SpaceX. Basically, instead of trying to develop an ambitious technology in one shot, start with a simpler, less ambitious version of it, and advance via learning by doing. “...much like the Starship example, starting with the end state and trying to solve all the various technology challenges all in one go would be incredibly challenging. So Fervo has opted to take a learning by doing path that parallels SpaceX. Project Red was our first pilot. Rather than try to drill a super hot or super deep concept right out of the gate, we completed a project in a category called “near-field Enhanced Geothermal Systems” (NF-EGS). This meant going to a location that was adjacent to a producing geothermal site, so the geothermal gradient was higher, even though the permeability in the part of the field we had selected did not support prior development with conventional technology.” [LinkedIn]

translations: 欢迎来到阅读清单，这是一份关于建筑、基础设施和工业技术的每周新闻与链接汇总。本周我们关注中国电动汽车补贴、航改型燃气轮机的未来、美沙核协议、有缺陷的道路护栏等。大约三分之二的阅读清单内容设有付费墙，如需获取完整访问权限，请成为付费订阅者。
美国最大的住宅建筑商 DR Horton 的首席执行官认为，《21世纪住房道路法案》在短期内不会对住房供需产生太大影响。[X]
《金融时报》探讨了为什么社会主义者应该拥抱豪华公寓。“最重要的是，高端开发项目能解锁长住房链条。随着高收入家庭搬入新建单元，他们腾出了老旧房产，通过一种被称为‘过滤’的过程，增加了中低端住房的供应并降低了价格。许多国际研究都强调了这种积极的连锁反应。”这是一种很好的观点，不过对《金融时报》的读者说这些，大概是在向已经认同的人说教。[FT]
上周我们提到，原本计划成为 California Forever 造船厂主要租户的 Saronic，最终选择将其业务设在德克萨斯州。有人在 Twitter 上声称，事实上加州从未真正被纳入考虑范围，向 California Forever 示好完全是为了在德克萨斯州争取更好的条件。[X]
通过 ResiClub 的数据，展示美国房价上涨与下跌的住房市场比例随时间的变化。[X]
曾经拥有至少 10 万人口但如今不再有的美国城市。[Reddit]
由于 AI 需求巨大，台积电（TSMC）正在加速其在亚利桑那州晶圆厂的投资。[CNBC] 此外，台积电计划从 2027 年起将价格上调最高 10%。[Yahoo Finance]
随着中国电动汽车产业日益成熟，中国开始削减对该行业的补贴。“根据财政部周五的公告，从 9 月 1 日起，锂电池将被征收 2% 的消费税，一年后将翻倍至 4%。”[X]

《国家历史保护法》（NHPA）要求考虑新项目是否会影响某些现有历史建筑的景观。因此，项目占地越广或高度越高，潜在的景观影响就越大，NHPA 的审查负担也就越重。这对风能和太阳能等清洁能源项目来说是个坏消息，因为它们的“景观足迹”比石油和天然气项目大得多。“我们考察了近 100 个最近的能源项目，发现了一个惊人的差异：与化石能源项目相比，清洁能源和输电项目的审查区域大约大 10 倍，且收到‘不利影响’裁定的可能性高出 8 倍以上——这会引发额外的程序、延误和缓解义务。”[IFP]

地热初创公司 Fervo Energy 的首席执行官 Tim Latimer 谈到了地热行业可以从 SpaceX 身上学到什么。基本上，不要试图一次性开发出雄心勃勃的技术，而是从更简单、目标更低的版本起步，通过实践学习来不断推进。“……就像星舰（Starship）的例子一样，如果一开始就瞄准最终状态，试图一次性解决所有各种技术挑战，那将极其困难。因此，Fervo 选择了一条与 SpaceX 类似的‘在实践中学习’的道路。Project Red 是我们的首个试点项目。我们没有一开始就尝试超高温或超深度的钻探概念，而是完成了一个属于‘近场增强型地热系统’（NF-EGS）类别的项目。这意味着我们要去一个与正在生产的地热场地相邻的地点，那里的地热梯度更高，尽管我们选定区域的渗透性无法支持用传统技术进行先前的开发。” [LinkedIn]
